title: Machine learning-based risk prediction model for postoperative acute kidney injury in surgical patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD): development, validation, and SHAP-based explainability

paragraphs.en: Postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) is no longer regarded as a random postoperative complication; rather, it represents a predictable perioperative emergency that unfolds within a fragile physiological environment characterized by reduced nephron reserves, impaired autoregulation, and heightened vulnerability to hemodynamic and inflammatory stressors [1–4]. In CKD patients, even subtle perioperative perturbations may trigger rapid deterioration in renal function, suggesting that AKI follows discernible and potentially modifiable trajectories rather than unpredictably [5,6]. Consequently, modern perioperative nephrology increasingly demands forward-looking, real-time intelligence systems capable of anticipating evolving renal stress and initiating preemptive protective strategies before irreversible injury occurs [7,8]. Against this backdrop, machine learning-based prediction represents a critical first step toward transforming AKI prevention from reactive risk estimation to proactive, anticipatory renal protection.

Patients with CKD are particularly vulnerable to postoperative AKI because of reduced nephron reserves, impaired autoregulation, and increased susceptibility to hemodynamic fluctuations and nephrotoxic exposure [9–11]. Evidence suggests that even minor renal insults can lead to persistent kidney dysfunction, potentially accelerating progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) [12,13]. The occurrence of postoperative AKI in CKD patients has been strongly associated with increased in-hospital mortality, prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) stay, and greater long-term dialysis dependence [14–16].

Beyond its short-term clinical burden, AKI may serve as a “second hit” in CKD patients, exacerbating tubular injury and maladaptive repair, thereby hastening progression to chronic renal failure [17,18]. Recent mechanistic studies have identified key contributors, including mitochondrial dysfunction, microvascular rarefaction, and persistent inflammation [19–21]. These findings highlight the need for early identification of AKI risk in patients with CKD, particularly during the perioperative period when physiological perturbations are most pronounced.

Despite the clinical importance of this issue, there remains a lack of validated predictive tools tailored to surgical patients with preexisting CKD. Most existing AKI prediction approaches are static, single-time-point models that estimate the risk rather than anticipate the dynamic physiological deterioration that unfolds during surgery. They rely primarily on tabular variables and do not leverage multimodal perioperative data, such as arterial waveform features, ultrasound-derived renal hemodynamics, or metabolomic stress markers. This limits their ability to provide forward-looking, real-time kidney-protective intelligence, an essential requirement for high-risk CKD patients whose renal reserve and autoregulatory capacity are profoundly impaired. These models often neglect CKD-specific variables or fail to account for the nonlinear associations between perioperative parameters and renal outcomes. Additionally, few models incorporate postoperative AKD or long-term CKD progression endpoints, further limiting their clinical utility [22–24].

Advances in electronic health record mining and machine learning (ML) have facilitated the construction of flexible high-dimensional prediction models [25–27]. Prior studies applying the Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression, decision trees, and ensemble ML methods have shown promising results in predicting AKI and AKD in surgical settings [28,29]. However, external validation remains limited, and prediction models specifically targeting postoperative AKI in CKD patients are virtually absent.

The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database provides a rich and granular dataset encompassing pre-, intra-, and postoperative variables for ICU patients. Using this database, we aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model for predicting postoperative AKI in surgical patients with CKD. While the present model focuses on tabular clinical data, it serves as a foundational step toward next-generation dynamic, multimodal, and clinically integrated perioperative kidney protection systems. Our approach integrates logistic regression, ensemble learning, and restricted cubic spline (RCS) functions to assess nonlinear associations with the ultimate goal of providing clinically interpretable and actionable predictions to support perioperative decision-making and improve renal outcomes.

This retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the MIMIC-IV database (version 2.2), a publicly available and de-identified critical care database developed by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Laboratory for Computational Physiology. The database contains comprehensive clinical information from patients admitted to the intensive care units (ICUs) of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) between 2008 and 2019.

MIMIC-IV includes detailed data, such as patient demographics, diagnoses, medications, vital signs, laboratory test results, procedural records, fluid input/output, and in-hospital outcomes. Version 2.2 also incorporates surgical information and structured chart events and enables the study of perioperative risk factors in patients undergoing surgery. All data in the database were fully de-identified according to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) regulations.

Access to the database was granted after completion of the required Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI) course. The author of this study obtained access to credentials (certification ID: 69,379,488) and adhered to all data usage policies. Given the public and anonymized nature of the database, this study was exempt from institutional review board (IRB) approval.

Adult patients (aged ≥18 years) with preexisting CKD were included in this study. CKD was defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for more than 3 months prior to surgery, or a documented diagnosis of CKD based on the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-9/ICD-10) codes. Patients who underwent at least one surgical procedure during hospitalization and had complete perioperative data were eligible. Only the first surgical episode was considered for patients who underwent multiple surgeries during the same hospital stay. Exclusion criteria included patients with AKI prior to surgery and those with a hospital stay shorter than 48 h. Patients undergoing maintenance dialysis prior to surgery were excluded, as the KDIGO criteria for AKI are not applicable to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), and serum creatinine levels may fluctuate substantially between dialysis sessions independent of acute renal injury. The final study cohort was selected on the basis of these criteria.

The primary outcome of this study was the incidence of postoperative AKI, defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. AKI was diagnosed if any of the following were met: an increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, an increase to ≥1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for at least 6 consecutive hours.

Based on clinical experience and previously published literature [26–30], we extracted a comprehensive set of candidate predictor variables from the MIMIC-IV database to construct a risk-prediction model. These variables were categorized into five domains. First, demographic information, including age, sex, weight, and body mass index (BMI), was collected to account for the baseline characteristics. Second, comorbid conditions were extracted, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, congestive heart failure, CKD stage, myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular disease, and chronic liver disease, given their known association with increased AKI risk. Third, a panel of preoperative laboratory values was included to capture patients’ baseline physiological status. These variables included serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), electrolytes (e.g., sodium, potassium, phosphorus), serum albumin, hemoglobin, white blood cell count, and eGFR calculated using the CKD-EPI formula. Fourth, vital signs and clinical severity scores were incorporated, including systolic and diastolic blood pressure, mean arterial pressure (MAP), Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, and Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (SAPS II). Finally, surgical and perioperative variables were collected, including the type of surgery (e.g., cardiac and abdominal), urgency of the procedure (elective or emergency), operative time, intraoperative fluid administration, blood transfusion, use of vasopressors, and mechanical ventilation status. These intraoperative and perioperative predictors were incorporated to reflect the multifactorial pathophysiology leading to postoperative AKI in surgical patients with preexisting CKD. In accordance with the data availability in the MIMIC-IV database, urine output criteria were not applied because perioperative urine output records were not consistently or reliably documented. Therefore, the AKI diagnosis in this study was based solely on the KDIGO serum creatinine criteria.

To ensure data completeness and minimize information bias, a variable-level missing data strategy was applied. Candidate predictors with more than 30% missingness were excluded a priori, as severe incompleteness or inconsistent documentation would compromise the data quality and model interpretability. Therefore, several clinically important variables within these categories were not included in the final analysis, including intraoperative blood loss, anesthesia technique, complete perioperative fluid balance, intraoperative urine output, detailed anesthetic drug types or doses, vasopressor infusion rates, temperature management parameters, and intraoperative hemodynamic variability (e.g., duration of hypotension). Variables with less than 30% missingness were imputed using the MissForest algorithm.

To reduce model complexity and enhance predictive generalizability, two complementary feature selection methods were applied: LASSO and the Boruta algorithm. LASSO regression was conducted using the “glmnet” package in R with 10-fold cross-validation. The optimal penalty parameter (λ) was selected based on the minimum mean cross-validated error, and features with nonzero coefficients at λ were retained. The Boruta algorithm was used to perform the wrapper-based feature selection. Implemented via the “Boruta” package in R, it evaluates all variables against randomly permuted shadow features and iteratively eliminates those that are statistically unimportant.

A suite of predictive models to estimate the risk of postoperative AKI in surgical CKD patients was developed. The following models were constructed and compared: logistic regression (baseline model), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and light-gradient boosting machine (LightGBM). In total, nine machine-learning algorithms were evaluated. Logistic regression analysis was performed using the “stats” package in R. Machine learning models were implemented using the “randomForest,” “xgboost,” and “lightgbm” package in R. Hyperparameter tuning was performed via a grid search combined with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. The dataset was randomly split into 70% training and 30% testing sets with stratification based on AKI status to ensure a balanced outcome distribution. All continuous variables were standardized or normalized as appropriate. In addition, five commonly used machine learning classifiers—support vector machine (SVM), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), multilayer perceptron (MLP), AdaBoost, and Naive Bayes—were included as benchmark models to comprehensively compare the performance of different modeling approaches.

Model performance was assessed by calculating the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score. Calibration was evaluated using the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test and visualized with calibration plots. Decision curve analysis (DCA) was conducted to evaluate the net clinical benefit of each model across a range of threshold probabilities. To enhance the model interpretability, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were applied to the final XGBoost model. The SHAP values quantify the contribution of each feature to individual predictions, allowing both global feature importance rankings and local risk explanations for individual patients.

Continuous variables are summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for normally distributed data or median with interquartile range (IQR) for non-normal data. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between the AKI and non-AKI groups were performed using the Student’s t-test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate. Multicollinearity among the predictors was assessed using the variance inflation factor (VIF), with a threshold of VIF >5 indicating potential collinearity. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.2.2) and Python (version 3.9) with the relevant packages, including glmnet, Boruta, randomForest, XGBoost, lightgbm, SHAP, pROC, caret, and rmda. A two-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The data used were derived from the publicly available and de-identified MIMIC-IV database, which received approval from the Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) of MIT and BIDMC. The author completed the required Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI) program and obtained access to the database (Certification ID: 69,379,488). Owing to the anonymized and publicly accessible nature of the data, this study was exempt from additional IRB approval.

A total of 3,851 surgical patients with preexisting chronic kidney disease (CKD) were included in the analysis. Among them, 932 patients (24.2%) developed postoperative AKI, as defined by the KDIGO criteria.

The median age of the cohort was 67.0 years (IQR: 58.0–76.0), with 58.7% being male. Patients in the AKI group were older than those in the non-AKI group (median 69.0 vs. 65.0 years, p < 0.001) and had a higher prevalence of comorbidities, including congestive heart failure (26.9 vs. 18.6%, p < 0.001), diabetes mellitus (37.6 vs. 29.8%, p = 0.002), and hypertension (71.2 vs. 63.9%, p = 0.008).

The laboratory and physiological parameters also showed significant differences. The AKI group had higher preoperative serum creatinine (median 2.1 vs. 1.5 mg/dL, p < 0.001), lower eGFR (43.1 vs. 56.7 mL/min/1.73 m2, p < 0.001), lower serum albumin (3.1 vs. 3.8 g/dL, p < 0.001), and higher SOFA and SAPS II scores (mean SOFA 6.3 vs. 4.2, p < 0.001). Additionally, intraoperative exposures, such as vasopressor use, mechanical ventilation, and emergency surgery, were significantly more common among patients who developed AKI (Table 1).

sections.title: Prediction performance of machine learning models on the validation set

paragraphs.en: The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves of the nine machine learning models are presented in Figure 1, illustrating their ability to discriminate between patients with and without postoperative AKI. Among all the models, XGBoost achieved the highest AUC of 0.844, indicating excellent discriminatory performance. This was followed by Random Forest (AUC = 0.822) and LightGBM (AUC = 0.804), both of which showed strong prediction capabilities. Traditional logistic regression and SVM also demonstrated comparable performances, with AUCs of 0.793 and 0.791, respectively. KNN and MLP showed moderate performance (AUC = 0.795 and 0.782, respectively), whereas AdaBoost and Naive Bayes yielded lower AUC values of 0.656 and 0.636, respectively, suggesting limited discriminative power. Overall, the ROC analysis highlighted that ensemble-based models, particularly XGBoost and Random Forest, outperformed conventional classifiers in predicting postoperative AKI in patients with CKD.

The predictive performance of the nine machine learning models was evaluated using five key metrics: accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score. The results are shown in Figure 2. Among all the models, XGBoost consistently outperformed the others, achieving the highest values across nearly all metrics, including AUC (0.844), accuracy (0.791), sensitivity (0.79), specificity (0.80), and F1-score (0.73). Random Forest and LightGBM also demonstrated strong predictive abilities, with AUCs of 0.822 and 0.804, respectively, and F1-scores of 0.68 and 0.70, respectively. The logistic regression model achieved moderate performance (accuracy, 0.733; AUC, 0.793; F1-score, 0.62), whereas MLP and SVM also showed balanced but slightly lower predictive values. In contrast, Naive Bayes and AdaBoost exhibit poor performance. Naive Bayes yielded the lowest AUC (0.636) and F1-score (0.57), whereas AdaBoost showed lower accuracy (0.754) and sensitivity (0.69) than the other models. Overall, tree-based ensemble models (XGBoost, Random Forest, and LightGBM) performed better than traditional classifiers in predicting postoperative AKI with higher discriminative power and classification balance.

The calibration of the best-performing model by using a calibration curve was assessed (Figure 3). Predicted probabilities were plotted against observed event frequencies. The results showed that the calibration curve closely followed the 45-degree diagonal reference line, indicating good agreement between the predicted and actual probabilities of postoperative AKI. Minor deviations from the ideal line were observed in certain probability ranges. However, the overall trend demonstrated that the model’s predicted risk was generally consistent with the true event probability. This suggests that the model not only discriminates well but also provides well-calibrated probability estimates suitable for clinical risk stratification.

The XGBoost algorithm was used to assess the contribution of each variable in the prediction of postoperative AKI. The feature importance was calculated based on the average gain, which reflects the relative contribution of each feature to the model. As shown in Figure 4, the SOFA score was the most important predictor (gain = 0.119), followed by eGFR (0.110), systolic blood pressure (0.094), serum albumin (0.091), and serum phosphorus (0.078). Other variables with relatively high importance included WBC count, BMI, and BUN level. These findings suggest that organ function indicators and preoperative physiological status play key roles in predicting the risk of AKI in surgical patients with CKD.

To further interpret the contribution and directionality of each predictor, SHAP analysis was performed based on the XGBoost model. The SHAP beeswarm plot in Figure 5 illustrates the distribution and impact of each feature across the individual predictions. Each dot represents a patient, and the position on the x-axis reflects the SHAP value for that feature in that individual. Features were ordered by their overall importance, with SOFA, eGFR, SBP, and albumin showing the greatest influence.

The color gradient (from purple to yellow) represents the original feature values, where yellow indicates high values and purple indicates low values. Notably, higher SOFA scores (yellow dots) were associated with an increased risk of AKI, while higher eGFR values (yellow dots) were associated with a lower risk. This suggests that worsening organ dysfunction and renal impairment are closely associated with AKI development. SHAP analysis not only confirmed the importance ranking from the gain-based analysis but also provided interpretability at the individual prediction level.

This study developed and validated nine machine-learning models to predict postoperative AKI in surgical patients with preexisting CKD. By leveraging routinely available clinical, laboratory, and physiological variables, the models demonstrated promising discriminatory and calibration performance, highlighting the potential of data-driven approaches for early risk stratification in high-risk surgical populations. The overall incidence of postoperative AKI in our cohort was 24.2%, which is comparable to that reported in previous studies involving patients with underlying CKD [30,31]. Patients who developed AKI had a higher burden of comorbidities, more severe baseline physiological derangement, and greater exposure to intraoperative stressors, all of which are well-established contributors to renal vulnerability during and after surgery [32]. In summary, while the current model provides robust tabular-data-based prediction for postoperative AKI in patients with CKD, this study should be viewed as a springboard for next-generation dynamic, multimodal, and clinically integrated perioperative kidney protection systems.

Among the nine models evaluated, ensemble learning methods, particularly XGBoost and Random Forest, consistently outperformed traditional algorithms across all five performance metrics. XGBoost achieved the highest AUC (0.844), accuracy (0.791), sensitivity (0.79), and F1-score (0.73), indicating a superior discriminatory ability and balance between precision and recall. These results align with those of previous studies showing that ensemble algorithms, by aggregating multiple weak learners, can capture nonlinear and complex interactions among clinical predictors more effectively than logistic regression or support vector machines [33,34]. Naive Bayes demonstrated lower performance, likely due to its strong assumption of conditional independence among predictors, which is inconsistent with the correlated biochemical and physiological variables in clinical datasets. AdaBoost is sensitive to noise and class imbalance, which may have contributed to its reduced performance in this cohort.

Importantly, our SHAP analysis revealed that SOFA score, eGFR, systolic blood pressure, albumin level, and phosphorus level were the top five most influential predictors. The SOFA score reflects multiorgan dysfunction and is an established prognostic marker in critically ill patients [35–37]. Lower eGFR and albumin levels suggest impaired baseline renal function and nutritional status, both of which are independently associated with an increased AKI risk. Meanwhile, lower systolic blood pressure may reflect perioperative hemodynamic instability, which contributes to renal hypoperfusion and ischemic injury [38–40]. Elevated phosphorus levels, although less frequently discussed, may indicate underlying mineral metabolism disturbances and subclinical renal tubular damage [41,42].

The findings from both feature importance ranking and SHAP value visualization not only confirmed known risk factors but also enhanced interpretability at the individual level. This is particularly valuable in clinical settings, where personalized decision-making is essential. Beyond discrimination, the XGBoost model demonstrated favorable calibration characteristics, with predicted probabilities closely aligned with the observed AKI incidence. Calibration is a critical but often overlooked aspect of model performance. A well-calibrated model ensures that the predicted risks can be translated into actionable thresholds for clinical decision-making, such as intensified monitoring or nephroprotective interventions [43–47].

This study contributes to the growing body of literature that advocates machine learning for perioperative risk prediction. Notably, our focus on a CKD population, a group underrepresented in many prediction studies, addresses an important gap. As one of the few studies specifically targeting postoperative AKI in surgical patients with preexisting CKD, our work expands the current evidence to a uniquely high-risk and understudied population. Patients with CKD are inherently more susceptible to AKI, and accurate risk estimation in this group may help tailor perioperative care such as nephrotoxin avoidance, optimized fluid management, and postoperative surveillance [47,48]. This model supports perioperative decision-making by enabling early AKI prevention strategies, potentially reducing the progression to dialysis and mortality. This model can inform AI-powered perioperative decision support systems for AKI prevention in patients with CKD. This SHAP-explainable machine learning model could be embedded into perioperative electronic health records (EHR) dashboards for proactive AKI prevention in patients with CKD.

From a practical perspective, the models developed in this study can be integrated into clinical workflows using EHRs as real-time risk calculators. Such tools, combined with SHAP-based interpretability, could assist clinicians in understanding not only the predicted risk level but also the key driving factors behind it [49]. Our findings may serve as a scaffold for future multimodal AKI digital twin frameworks. Nonetheless, this study has several limitations. First, our analysis was based on retrospective data from a single center. Although internal validation was performed, external validation using independent datasets, such as MIMIC-IV or other multicenter databases, is necessary to confirm the generalizability [50]. Second, several perioperative variables of clinical relevance (e.g., blood loss, anesthesia type, and perioperative fluid balance) did not appear in the final model because they had excessive missingness or were not retained during model development. Third, although SHAP improves transparency, machine learning models remain inherently more complex than traditional logistic regression models, potentially posing barriers to clinical adoption. Additionally, the development and reporting of our model followed FAIR and provenance principles to ensure the transparency, reproducibility, and traceability of data processing and analytic workflows.

This study demonstrated that machine learning models, especially ensemble-based algorithms such as XGBoost and Random Forest, can effectively predict postoperative AKI in surgical patients with CKD using preoperative clinical data. Explainable AI techniques further enhance clinical interpretability. XGBoost with SHAP interpretability provides explainable AKI signals that are suitable for LLM-based clinical reasoning. Future work should focus on external validation, prospective implementation, and the development of user-friendly decision support tools to facilitate clinical translation. These results could inform digital twin–based perioperative renal monitoring systems or serve as input features for LLM-based autonomous decision support agents. Future prospective trials are needed to evaluate whether EHR-integrated AI risk alerts can prompt early fluid optimization, vasopressor titration, and nephrotoxin avoidance in patients with CKD.

sections.title: Beyond tabular prediction: emerging directions for intelligent perioperative kidney protection

paragraphs.en: Future research should advance beyond the static, tabular-data-based prediction of dynamic, multimodal, and physiologically informed perioperative kidney-protection systems. One important direction is the development of perioperative digital renal twins, virtual physiological models capable of simulating renal perfusion, fluid status, and hemodynamic trajectories under different surgical stress conditions. These systems may allow the real-time assessment of renal vulnerability and support personalized nephroprotective strategies before irreversible injury occurs. AI-driven shared decision-making tools that visually present individualized kidney-risk trajectories to surgical teams and patients may further enhance transparency and coordinate perioperative planning.

Next-generation multimodal AI models can integrate arterial pressure waveform features (e.g., PPV, SVV, and dP/dt), ultrasound-derived renal resistive indices, real-time urinary or metabolomic biomarkers, and CT/MRI-based renal texture markers, providing a more comprehensive depiction of intraoperative renal stress than tabular variables alone. Prehabilitation-oriented AI systems can also estimate risk days before surgery and trigger early renal optimization strategies (e.g., nutritional enhancement, fluid preload targeting, anemia, or albumin correction) to strengthen renal resilience before operative stress.

Emerging transformer architectures, diffusion forecasting models, and reinforcement learning-based closed-loop decision support may further enable dynamic AKI trajectory prediction, simulation of “what-if” hemodynamic strategies, and autonomous optimization of fluid or vasopressor titrations. Incorporating continual or federated learning can ensure that perioperative AKI models evolve across institutions and over time rather than remaining static. Compared with traditional ensemble models, such as XGBoost or Random Forest, transformer-based multimodal foundation models offer substantially greater capacity for integrating heterogeneous perioperative signals and modeling complex temporal dependencies. Future work could also combine explainable AI methods, such as SHAP, with causal counterfactual analysis to generate actionable “what-if” simulations, for example, estimating how maintaining systolic blood pressure above specific thresholds might modify a patient’s predicted AKI trajectory. Embedding such predictive insights into EHR workflows as automated alerts paired with recommended intervention bundles is essential for real-world translational implementations. Ethical and regulatory readiness will also be crucial, including model drift monitoring, bias auditing, transparency requirements, and governance frameworks for adaptive or continuously learning perioperative AI systems. These advancements highlight the future in which perioperative kidney protection moves beyond prediction toward real-time, adaptive, and AI-integrated clinical decision systems for high-risk CKD patients.
Our explainable XGBoost model enables real-time perioperative AKI risk prediction in patients with CKD and may serve as a foundation for AI-guided decision support systems in surgical nephrology.

This study developed and validated multiple machine learning models to predict postoperative AKI in surgical patients with preexisting CKD based on data from the MIMIC-IV database. Our findings demonstrate that ensemble models, particularly XGBoost, achieve superior discrimination and calibration performance compared to traditional algorithms. Furthermore, the application of SHAP analysis enabled the interpretation of individual-level predictions and the identification of key risk factors, including SOFA score, eGFR, systolic blood pressure, albumin, and phosphorus. These results suggest that interpretable machine learning models may serve as valuable tools for perioperative risk stratification and the targeted prevention of AKI in high-risk surgical populations. Future work should focus on external validation, integration into clinical workflows, and the assessment of real-world impacts.
